chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Musa ibn Bakr, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman who is incapacitated (or a minor/mentally incompetent), and she has wealth in the hand of her brother. Is there zakat upon her? He said: 'If her brother trades with it, then there is zakat upon her.'

key_terms.مُصَابَةٍ: Incapacitated or afflicted (often referring to a minor or mentally incompetent person in fiqh contexts)
key_terms.يَتَّجِرُ بِهِ: He trades with it (engages in commercial activity)

ai.seo_question: Is zakat obligatory on the wealth of a minor or incapacitated woman if her guardian trades with it?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that the obligation of zakat on the wealth of minors or the incapacitated is contingent upon the wealth being 'active' or engaged in trade, rather than merely held in custody. It reflects the Shia juristic principle that zakat is a tax on productive capital, distinguishing between dormant assets and those generating profit through commercial activity.
